glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Solomon faces the death that comes to righteous and wicked alike and turns it into a call to receive life now as God’s gift, to eat with joy, love one’s wife, and work with all one’s might, then shows that skill cannot guarantee outcomes and that saving wisdom can still be despised.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 9 opens Ecclesiastes 9:1–10:20, the movement on the one event that comes to all and on wisdom and folly. Its opening words link back to 8:17, where Solomon admitted that no one can find out the work of God.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work or device or knowledge or wisdom in the grave where you are going.” (Ecclesiastes 9:10)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 9 begins with a confession of faith: “the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God” (verse 1). Then comes a hard fact. “One event happens to the righteous and the wicked” (verse 2). The good and the sinner remain morally different, but death comes to both. Seen only from under the sun, the dead “know nothing” and “Nevermore will they have a share In anything done under the sun” (verses 5–6). Verse 6 shows the limit of these words: they describe the end of earthly life, not a full account of life after death. The same book says that “the spirit will return to God who gave it” (12:7).

From that sober fact Solomon draws a surprising command. “Go, eat your bread with joy, And drink your wine with a merry heart; For God has already accepted your works” (verse 7). He calls his reader to dress for celebration, to live joyfully with the wife he loves, and to do whatever his hand finds to do “with your might” (verses 8–10). Death does not make life worthless. It makes the present precious, because the days God gives are the time to work and rejoice.

The rest of the chapter adds that no one controls outcomes. “The race is not to the swift, Nor the battle to the strong,” because “time and chance happen to them all” (verse 11). A poor wise man once saved a besieged city by his wisdom, “Yet no one remembered that same poor man” (verse 15). Wisdom is better than strength and weapons, even when people despise it.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 9:1–6 — One Event for All

The righteous and the wise are in God’s hand, yet the same death comes to good and evil alike, and the living still have hope that the dead have lost. Seen within the earthly horizon, the dead know nothing and no longer share in anything done under the sun, words that describe the end of earthly life, not a full teaching on the afterlife.

Ecclesiastes 9:7–10 — Receive Life as God’s Gift

Solomon calls his reader to eat and drink with joy, because God has already accepted his works, and to dress for celebration and live joyfully with the wife he loves as his portion in life. Whatever his hand finds to do, he should do it with all his strength, because work ends at the grave.

Ecclesiastes 9:11–12 — Time and Chance

Speed, strength, wisdom, understanding, and skill do not guarantee their expected rewards, because time and chance happen to everyone. Like fish caught in a net or birds in a snare, people are caught suddenly by an evil time they did not foresee.

Ecclesiastes 9:13–18 — The Poor Wise Man Forgotten

A great king besieged a little city, and a poor wise man delivered it by his wisdom, yet no one remembered him. Solomon concludes that wisdom is better than strength and weapons of war, though the poor man’s wisdom is despised and one sinner can destroy much good.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 9 lets the reality of death be felt, especially by those who grieve. It does not pretend that death is small. Yet it does not teach that death ends all existence. The statements about the dead describe their loss of earthly life, and the wider witness of Scripture speaks of conscious life with Christ after death (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23).

The chapter also frees believers to enjoy ordinary life. “God has already accepted your works” (9:7) is not a way to earn salvation, and it is not approval of everything a person does. It encourages people who fear God to receive meals, marriage, and work gratefully instead of suspecting that every joy displeases Him.

Finally, the forgotten poor wise man shows that wisdom can rescue people and still be overlooked. Read alongside the rest of Scripture, the story points to Christ, who became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), whose saving wisdom the world counted foolish (1 Corinthians 1:23–25), and who came to free people held under the power of death (Hebrews 2:14–15).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
One event for all. Death comes to the righteous and the wicked alike, though they are not alike before God (9:1–6).

Life received as God’s gift. Food, celebration, marriage, and work are to be received with joy while life lasts (9:7–10).

Work with all your might. The days before the grave are the time to do with full strength whatever one’s hand finds to do (9:10).

Time and chance. Skill and strength do not guarantee success, and misfortune can arrive suddenly (9:11–12).

Wisdom despised. Wisdom can save a city and still be forgotten, and one sinner can undo much good (9:13–18).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
In the hand of God (9:1). Under God’s care and control. Even when people cannot read what lies ahead, the righteous and the wise and their works belong to Him.

The dead know nothing (9:5). A statement about death seen from under the sun. Verse 6 limits it to having no further share in earthly life. It does not teach that the soul sleeps or ceases to exist (compare 12:7).

God has already accepted your works (9:7). Encouragement to receive ordinary life and faithful work with confidence in God’s favor. It is not salvation by works or approval of whatever anyone does (11:9; 12:13–14).

White garments and oil (9:8). Signs of celebration and gladness in the ancient world, worn on festive occasions.

Portion (9:9). A person’s God-given share in life. Here marriage and daily labor are named as gifts from God.

Time and chance (9:11). Unforeseen events that overturn human plans. The phrase describes life from the human point of view and does not place anything outside God’s rule (9:1).

Ecclesiastes 9:13–18 — The Poor Wise Man Forgotten

focus: Ecclesiastes 9 opens the movement “One Event for All; Wisdom and Folly” (9:1–10:20). The death that comes alike to righteous and wicked becomes a summons to receive life now as God’s gift, and the chapter then shows that neither skill nor saving wisdom can secure outcomes or honor.

sections.title: One Event for All
sections.summary: The righteous and the wise “are in the hand of God,” yet “One event happens to the righteous and the wicked.” A living dog is better than a dead lion, for “the dead know nothing” and nevermore have a share “In anything done under the sun.”

sections.title: Receive Life as God’s Gift
sections.summary: “Go, eat your bread with joy,” Solomon says, “For God has already accepted your works.” Wear white garments, live joyfully with the wife you love, and “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might,” because work ends at the grave.

sections.title: Time and Chance
sections.summary: “The race is not to the swift, Nor the battle to the strong,” for “time and chance happen to them all.” Like fish taken in a net or birds caught in a snare, people are caught “in an evil time, When it falls suddenly upon them.”

sections.title: The Poor Wise Man Forgotten
sections.summary: A poor wise man “by his wisdom delivered the city. Yet no one remembered that same poor man.” Solomon concludes that wisdom is better than strength and “better than weapons of war,” though “the poor man’s wisdom is despised” and “one sinner destroys much good.”

1.brief: After reflecting on all this, Solomon declares that “the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God.” Even so, no one can tell from present circumstances whether love or hatred awaits him.
1.explain:
For I considered all this in my heart, so that I could declare it all: links this chapter to the conclusion of 8:17 that no one can find out God’s work. Solomon has reflected carefully and now states what he has concluded.

that the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God. affirms that the righteous and the wise, and everything they do, rest under God’s sovereign care and control. Their lives are not left to blind fate.

People know neither love nor hatred by anything they see before them. adds that no one can tell from present circumstances whether God’s favor or disfavor lies ahead. Outward events do not reveal God’s disposition toward a person.
1.notes: The Hebrew of the last line is brief and can also be read to mean that people do not know whether love or hatred awaits them in the future. Both readings stress the limits of what people can know from circumstances.

2.brief: “One event happens to the righteous and the wicked,” to the clean and unclean, the worshiper and the one who never sacrifices. Death comes to all alike, whatever their character or religious practice.
2.explain:
All things come alike to all: introduces the observation that the same outcome comes to everyone.

One event happens to the righteous and the wicked; names that outcome, death, which comes to righteous and wicked alike.

To the good, the clean, and the unclean; extends the list. Moral and ceremonial differences do not change the common end.

To him who sacrifices and him who does not sacrifice. adds religious practice. The worshiper and the one who neglects worship both die.

As is the good, so is the sinner; summarizes the point.

He who takes an oath as he who fears an oath. adds one more pair: the one who swears carelessly and the one who treats oaths with reverence. Death does not distinguish them. The righteous and the wicked remain morally different; they simply share the same physical death.

3.brief: Solomon calls it an evil that one fate comes to everyone, and he adds that human hearts are full of evil and madness while they live, and then they go to the dead. Shared death and shared sinfulness mark every human life.
3.explain:
This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: calls the common fate of death an evil. Within earthly life, it seems wrong that death treats everyone the same.

that one thing happens to all. restates the problem.

Truly the hearts of the sons of men are full of evil; adds a diagnosis of human hearts. People are full of evil.

madness is in their hearts while they live, describes folly and moral confusion that mark human life.

and after that they go to the dead. ends the sentence with death. A life marked by sin and folly ends at the grave.

4.brief: Yet while a person is alive “there is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.” Even the lowest living creature has opportunities that the mightiest dead one has lost.
4.explain:
But for him who is joined to all the living there is hope, turns to the value of being alive. While a person lives, there is still hope and opportunity.

for a living dog is better than a dead lion. gives a vivid comparison. In Israel dogs were despised scavengers and lions were symbols of strength and majesty. Yet a living dog is better off than a dead lion, because life still holds possibilities that death has ended.

5.brief: The living know that they will die, but “the dead know nothing,” have no further reward, and are forgotten. Within the earthly horizon of Solomon’s examination, death ends a person’s knowledge of and part in life under the sun; it does not teach that the soul ceases to exist.
5.explain:
For the living know that they will die; says the living at least know something: that death is coming. That knowledge can guide how they live.

But the dead know nothing, says the dead have no knowledge. This describes death within the earthly horizon of Solomon’s examination: the dead have no awareness of or part in life under the sun. Verse 6 makes that limit explicit. The verse does not teach that the soul sleeps or ceases to exist; the same book says that “the spirit will return to God who gave it” (12:7).

And they have no more reward, adds that the dead receive no further earthly wages or gain.

For the memory of them is forgotten. adds that even their memory fades among the living.
5.notes: The Hebrew words for “reward” (sakar) and “memory” (zeker) sound alike, so the last two lines contain a play on words.

6.brief: The love, hatred, and envy of the dead have perished, and “Nevermore will they have a share In anything done under the sun.” This verse defines what the dead have lost: their share in earthly life, not their existence before God.
6.explain:
Also their love, their hatred, and their envy have now perished; says the passions that drove the dead in life are gone.

Nevermore will they have a share In anything done under the sun. defines the scope of what the dead have lost. They no longer share in earthly affairs “under the sun.” This qualifies verse 5 and shows that Solomon speaks of earthly participation, not of existence before God. Scripture elsewhere speaks of conscious life with Christ after death (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23).

7.brief: Solomon says, “Go, eat your bread with joy, And drink your wine with a merry heart; For God has already accepted your works.” In this setting, the words encourage a person to receive ordinary life and faithful labor with assurance of God’s favor; they do not describe a way of earning salvation.
7.explain:
Go, eat your bread with joy, turns from death to a call to enjoy life. Ordinary food is to be eaten with gladness.

And drink your wine with a merry heart; adds wine, a common sign of celebration, enjoyed with a glad heart.

For God has already accepted your works. gives the reason. Because God has accepted the works of those who fear Him, the reader can receive ordinary life and faithful work with gladness and with assurance of His favor, rather than suspecting that every enjoyment displeases Him. This does not describe a way of earning salvation, and it is not blanket approval of wickedness, since the book holds every work accountable to God (12:14).

8.brief: White garments and oil on the head were signs of festivity and gladness. Solomon urges a life marked by joy rather than by gloom.
8.explain:
Let your garments always be white, urges festive dress. In a hot climate, white garments reflected the sun and were worn on joyful occasions.

And let your head lack no oil. adds oil for the head, a sign of refreshment and celebration. Together the images describe a life marked by gladness rather than gloom. The verse speaks of ordinary festivity, not of explicit spiritual symbols.

9.brief: Live joyfully with the wife you love all the days of your fleeting life, because she is your God-given portion in life and in your labor. Marriage is one of the gifts God gives within a brief life.
9.explain:
Live joyfully with the wife whom you love calls for joy in marriage. A loving wife is one of God’s great gifts in this life.

all the days of your vain life which He has given you under the sun, places marriage within life’s brevity. “Vain” here means fleeting, like a breath, and God is the giver of these days.

all your days of vanity; repeats the reminder that life is short.

for that is your portion in life, and in the labor which you perform under the sun. calls marriage a person’s portion, his God-given share in life and in his work. Because life is brief, its gifts should be received with gratitude now.

10.brief: Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength, because there is no work or planning or knowledge in the grave. Life’s opportunities are limited, so they should be used fully now.
10.explain:
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; calls for wholehearted effort in whatever task lies at hand.

for there is no work or device or knowledge or wisdom in the grave where you are going. gives the reason. In the grave there is no more work, planning, knowledge, or wisdom of the kind done under the sun. Life’s opportunities end at death, so they should be used fully now. As in verse 5, the statement describes the end of earthly activity, not a complete teaching about life after death.
10.notes: The Hebrew word translated “grave” is Sheol, the common Old Testament term for the realm of the dead.

11.brief: Solomon observes that the race does not always go to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, nor bread to the wise, nor riches to the discerning, nor favor to the skilled; “time and chance happen to them all.” Ability does not guarantee its expected reward, because unforeseen events can overturn human plans.
11.explain:
I returned and saw under the sun that introduces another observation.

The race is not to the swift, Nor the battle to the strong, observes that speed and strength do not always win.

Nor bread to the wise, Nor riches to men of understanding, Nor favor to men of skill; adds that wisdom, understanding, and skill do not guarantee food, wealth, or favor.

But time and chance happen to them all. gives the reason. Unforeseen events and circumstances affect everyone. This does not describe a universe outside God’s control, since verse 1 says the righteous and the wise are “in the hand of God.” It describes life as people experience it, where outcomes cannot be predicted. Proverbs describes the usual patterns of life, such as diligence leading to prosperity; Ecclesiastes adds that those patterns are not unconditional guarantees, and the two books complement each other.

12.brief: People do not know when their time will come; like fish caught in a cruel net or birds in a snare, they are trapped in an evil time that falls suddenly upon them. Disaster can come without warning to anyone.
12.explain:
For man also does not know his time: says no one knows when misfortune or death will come.

Like fish taken in a cruel net, Like birds caught in a snare, gives two pictures of sudden capture. Fish and birds are caught without warning.

So the sons of men are snared in an evil time, When it falls suddenly upon them. applies the pictures. People are overtaken by disaster unexpectedly.

13.brief: Solomon introduces an example of wisdom under the sun that seemed great to him. What follows is a small story with a large lesson.
13.explain:
This wisdom I have also seen under the sun, introduces a story that illustrates wisdom.

and it seemed great to me: says the example impressed Solomon. It teaches something significant about wisdom.

14.brief: A great king besieged a little city with few men and built great siegeworks against it. The odds were overwhelmingly against the city.
14.explain:
There was a little city with few men in it; describes a small, weak town.

and a great king came against it, introduces a powerful enemy.

besieged it, and built great snares around it. describes the siege. The king surrounded the city and built works against it, which the NKJV calls “snares,” picturing the city caught as in a trap. The odds were overwhelmingly against the city.
14.notes: Where the NKJV has “snares,” the NET renders the structures as “siege works,” and the ESV and NASB as “siegeworks,” taking them as works built against a besieged city.

15.brief: A poor wise man was found in the city, and he delivered it by his wisdom, yet no one remembered him. His wisdom saved the city, but his poverty kept him from being honored.
15.explain:
Now there was found in it a poor wise man, introduces the hero, a man with no wealth or status but with wisdom.

and he by his wisdom delivered the city. says his wisdom saved the city. The NKJV states that he delivered it.

Yet no one remembered that same poor man. reports the sad end. Though he saved the city, he was forgotten because he was poor. The immediate lesson concerns wisdom that saves yet is despised, the point verse 16 draws out. Read alongside the rest of Scripture, the story also offers a secondary picture. The small city, helpless before a mighty enemy, can picture humanity in need of rescue, and the poor wise man can picture Christ, who became poor and whose saving wisdom was counted foolishness (2 Corinthians 8:9; 1 Corinthians 1:23–25). Through His death He broke the power of death and set free those who were held in bondage all their lives by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15), delivering His people from sin and death. Like the poor man, He is often unremembered by the very people He came to deliver.
15.notes: The NET reads the verb as a possibility: the poor man “could have delivered the city by his wisdom,” but no one listened to him. That reading ties the story closely to verse 16, where the poor man’s wisdom is despised. The NKJV states that he delivered the city, and this study follows that reading.

16.brief: Solomon concludes that “Wisdom is better than strength,” yet the poor man’s wisdom is despised and his words are not heard. Wisdom is valuable, but people often ignore it when it comes from someone of low standing.
16.explain:
Then I said: “Wisdom is better than strength. draws the first lesson. Wisdom accomplished what military strength could not.

Nevertheless the poor man’s wisdom is despised, adds the sad qualification. People despise wisdom when it comes from someone poor.

And his words are not heard. completes the point. A poor person’s wise words are ignored.

17.brief: Quiet words of the wise deserve to be heard more than the shouting of a ruler among fools. Wisdom does not need to be loud to be worth hearing.
17.explain:
Words of the wise, spoken quietly, should be heard says quiet words of wisdom deserve attention.

Rather than the shout of a ruler of fools. contrasts them with the loud commands of a leader among fools. Volume and position do not make words wise.

18.brief: “Wisdom is better than weapons of war; But one sinner destroys much good.” Wisdom can accomplish more than force, yet one foolish or sinful person can undo much of the good that wisdom builds.
18.explain:
Wisdom is better than weapons of war; repeats the lesson of the story. Wisdom can accomplish more than military might.

But one sinner destroys much good.” adds a warning. One foolish or sinful person can undo much of the good that wisdom builds. This sets up the saying about dead flies spoiling perfume in 10:1.
